extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in academic ethics, plagiarism controversies, and Chinese academia
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and assessing criteria used to judge alleged academic plagiarism and institutional responses in a case-study format (Wang Hui). Focuses on citation practices, textual borrowing, intent, and procedural/institutional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbatim copying without attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbatim copying of passages from scholars like Li Zehou and American historian Lin Yusheng without quotation marks or footnotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among the alleged "over 30 instances of 'inappropriate citation'"; verbatim, unattributed passages are presented as a clear indicator of improper scholarly practice and potential plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraphrased arguments without proper attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Paraphrased arguments from Japanese scholar Maruyama Noboru's 1965 Lu Xun study without proper attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paraphrase that reproduces another scholar's argument or structure without citation is treated as an attribution failure; the case treats such paraphrasing as part of the substantive allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural similarities to earlier scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural similarities to earlier Chinese scholarship on Lu Xun's intellectual development timeline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not only verbatim copying but close structural/organizational re-use of prior scholarship is considered evidence of problematic borrowing rather than independent synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of disputed passages in later editions
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2004 revised edition retained most disputed passages; similar passages remained in post-2000 reprints without correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to correct or annotate disputed material in later editions is used as evidence undermining claims that issues were accidental or purely historical formatting errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation irregularities / formatting inconsistencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Wang Hui acknowledged "citation irregularities" and attributed them to "formatting inconsistencies" from merging dissertation footnotes into book form and to "technical errors" in 1980s Chinese academia's nascent citation standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framing treats some attribution problems as possibly technical or editorial mistakes rather than intentional plagiarism; evaluators must weigh whether irregularities plausibly result from formatting versus misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/contextual standards for citation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument by supporters that allegations ignored the "historical context" of 1980s Chinese academic practices, and that critics conflated "citation flaws" with deliberate plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging past work, consider contemporaneous citation norms and whether those norms reasonably excuse certain practices; this is presented as a mitigating evaluative factor by defenders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timelessness of basic scholarly ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterargument by 91 international scholars that "basic scholarly ethics are timeless," rejecting the "different era" justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard holds that core principles of attribution and honesty transcend historical or regional citation conventions; evaluators invoking this treat any unattributed borrowing as violating perennial ethical norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish citation flaws from deliberate plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Contention between parties about whether issues amounted to mere "citation flaws" versus "serious violations of academic norms" (deliberate plagiarism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should consider intent, pattern, and scope: isolated formatting errors differ from systematic unattributed reuse; the case emphasizes this distinction as central to judging severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for formal institutional investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Calls by critics (e.g., international scholars) for Tsinghua University to conduct a formal investigation into the allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formal, transparent institutional inquiry is presented as the appropriate procedural response when substantial allegations of academic misconduct are raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional procedural limits on retroactive reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Tsinghua and CASS declined to reopen Wang's 22-year-old dissertation case, stating no current university regulations mandated retroactive plagiarism reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional rules and statutes of limitations can limit remedial action; when evaluating outcomes, consider whether procedures allow or bar retrospective review and correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisor/supervisor oversight and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis that Wang Hui's doctoral thesis advisor Tang Tao and other mentors failed to spot flaws, possibly due to unfamiliarity, age, or excessive trust, thereby allowing problematic material to pass review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessing a dissertation's integrity may include evaluating the rigor of supervisory oversight and whether advisors fulfilled responsibilities to detect improper attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of political motivations and reputational/defamation claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Wang Hui suggested "political motivations behind the timing of allegations" and commissioned a law firm to warn that the accusations "may constitute defamation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual factors such as possible political motivations or legal/defamation concerns are cited as factors that can influence interpretation, public discourse, and institutional responses, though they do not by themselves resolve questions of academic conduct.
